utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I remind the witness that he took an oath -- I beg your pardon, made a declaration yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth, and he's still bound by that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As far as I can remember, Your Honours, yesterday we were in private session. I believe it would be a good idea if we continued the same way because of the nature of the questions I'm going to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. And Mr. Milovancevic, may I remind you once again you've got to stick to questions related to the Martic police. We've got to finish with this witness as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in Saborsko, you mentioned that when you -- you attacked that place, there was -- there were some other soldiers on the other side. Now, you testified -- you said there were soldiers from on the other side and you were not able to see them. Which soldiers were these that you said were on the other side of Saborsko when you attacked Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the same army. It's just that these forces were taking a different route that I couldn't see from my vantage point because of the lay of the terrain. If you're referring to that attack from the direction of Plaski. Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your testimony was that you and 20 or 30 soldiers gathered in Licka Jesenica and that you could not see the police because they were on the other side. You were talking about the police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You see, all of us were gathered in Licka Jesenica. Now, when we set off to mount this attack, then every group belonging to this army took a different route as part of this attack. My group went along the route that I described yesterday, and for this reason I was unable to see that. I could see the military hardware and the army, but I told you that from my vantage point we could see the hamlet of Tuk and we could see the Serb army arriving and entering the hamlet of Tuk. As soon as they entered this hamlet, it was set alight. And that happened with another hamlet as well. That was what I was trying to describe. Of course, I couldn't see who set the hamlet on fire. I couldn't see the person setting it alight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question simply is: Who are these police who were on the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police that was commanded by Dusko Latas. If you remember, I said that when the municipalities split up, or rather, when the elections took place, the municipality of Ogulin set up another police department, or rather, approximately 12 to 15 men who worked there. They had their reserve force too there. And there was Martic's police that was commanded by Medakovic. Those were the police forces. But they had the same task. They were at the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Towards the end of questions by Defence counsel, you made a statement that whenever there was looting, their names would be mentioned concerning things like that. Now you were talking about these men who were -- you said were always around Ogrizovic. Were there many such lootings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not speak about all of them. But when these villages fell, Rakovica, Slunj, Saborsko, Poljanak, I mean, that's about it, that's the area. Then -- well, you know, it's not only them. There were ordinary other people too there who were in that area where the lootings took place, you see, but these were the most important ones. Everything hinged on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I do want to know is whether there were many such lootings in which Martic's police were involved.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few. I think there were quite a few. But I would like to say, I would like to note, that this group of people -- well, it's not that only those people were Martic's police. It wasn't only that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that it was not only that group. But I want -- the other groups are not before us. I'm interested in Martic's police. Martic's police were always involved; is that correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please understand what I'm saying. It wasn't only that group that was Martic's police. There were other people in Martic 's police too for whom I can guarantee that they were honourable men and who would not allow themselves to do that, but out of this Martic's police, there was this group that was inclined to do that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can I just get clarity on this Plascanska Brigade. Is that the same thing as the Plaski TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question. Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. There has been reference to Plascanska Brigade. What is this Plascanska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, that? Well I don't know exactly. I don't know exactly whether that group came before the attack on Saborsko or immediately after the attack on Saborsko. These were officers of the Yugoslav People's Army who took over the command, the entire command over this Territorial Defence. And that's when it was called the 124th Light Infantry Brigade, and as for long as there was a TO, Territorial Defence, in these barracks, there were only a few people, but when the brigade came, then there was this administration and then technical equipment was brought in. Perhaps seven or eight tanks, a few combat vehicles, and that's where the biggest warehouse was, and food was there too. I wanted to say that it started looking like a serious military formation then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was not the same thing as the Plaski TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, but I cannot claim with certainty -- well, I cannot. I cannot now, but I think that at that time that brigade had already been established, that these officers from Belgrade came. Officers came from Belgrade. 18 of them. I know that for sure. And they didn't have equipment yet. Cedo Bulat was very close to Plaski and there was a very big military formation there, so this formation of Plaski was under the command, I think, of this military command at the training grounds. I know very well that all the technical equipment came in from the training grounds when the attack on Saborsko took place; tanks and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm thinking. Yes, Your Honour, just one or two, and if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to the question that was put to you by the Honourable Judge Moloto in relation to what happened in Saborsko and the death of Pero Krtan, you described the people who did that. You said that they were in Ogrizovic's group, and in response to the question put by the Court, who they were, you said, "I think they were in this group of Martic's." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, in the statement that you gave to the police station in Karlovac, that is the 8th of November 1999, on page 1, you said, when talking about Ogrizovic's group, and the men belonging to it: "I don't know whether, with Martic or with Snjaka, this Pejic was there, and then in that group around Snjaka there were some Cvekic men, I mean Mane Cvekic and another called Trbojevic, also known as Ckalja." Now, what is correct, do you know or do you think that they belonged to Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, Martic's police, as it was called, Martic's police, this group, these men, I don't know how many there were but certainly there weren't many of them. In that group, there was always Snjaka and Cvekic and Pejic and Lecin. I mean, I'm talking about that group that did the greatest harm in that area of Plaski, that's what I'm saying. Now, I don't know, I do not know exactly who played which role and whether they were all involved in training and whether they were all with Martic, but I'm just saying that it was always that group and that is why we kept saying it was Martic's group. Now whether they exactly belonged to Martic's group, I don't know. I'm not claiming that. I never claimed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While answering the questions of the Honourable Trial Chamber about what happened in Josipdol and Ogulin, you said that from time to time they shelled Plaski and that fire was returned then. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I never said that it was first Ogulin or Plaski. You wouldn't know that. Sometimes Plaski would shell them and then they would return fire, and then they would fire at Plaski and then Plaski would fire back. And that's the way it went practically throughout the war, as far as this side is concerned, but there were no attempts made vis-a-vis Ogulin either from the Croat side or the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to the question put by the Trial Chamber as to who it was that attacked Josipdol and Ogulin, you said the Serb forces. And in response to the questions put by the Trial Chamber as to whether Martic's police was involved in these Serb forces, your answer was yes. But you also said that they were only attacked by artillery fire. Did the Martic police have artillery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that -- well, I wanted to say explicitly several times that there were never infantry attempts to attack Josipdol. Well, meaning shelling. That form of attack. That was from the Serb side in Plaski and in the Serb forces there was the Martic police too. They were part of the general armed forces of Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You did not answer my question. This group of policemen that was training in Knin that was called the Martic police, did they have artillery or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your microphone. You may proceed, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That group, well, had mortars of 60 millimetres. They were a mobile unit that was mobile. I mean, they didn't have tanks, they didn't have howitzers. They had only these mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this Martic's police, as you call it, took part in the attack on Ogulin? Do you have direct knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that. I always say that as far as Josipdol is concerned, it's never the infantry that moved against the place. And now whether they were shooting from mortars and who was shooting, howitzers were shooting too, and mortars of larger calibres. Now, that's the way Josipdol was attacked, and Ogulin too, but Martic's police could not attack Ogulin with small mortars if they used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. I thank you very much, Witness. That brings us to the end of your testimony. You are excused from further attending court. You may stand down. Thank you so much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Black will be handling the next witness, and with permission of the Chamber, could I be excused, please? But before I do that, I think with this next witness - and Mr. Black can address this more specifically - we are a little pressed for time with this next witness, and he's a 92 bis witness, cross only. It's our hope, if possible, to finish him by today. This is his second trip here because he was one of the witnesses who was here, ready to testify, when that week was cancelled. So if there is any way that that can be accommodated, it would be of great assistance to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, if the next witness could be brought in. His name is Neven Segaric. And I'll change positions here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Neven Segaric, solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. So help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may remain seated. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Segaric. I'm sorry we kept you waiting a little bit this morning. I know it's important for you to try to finish today, and we will make every effort to try to make that happen. Can you understand me clearly through the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If at any time you don't understand one of my questions, please just tell me and I'll try to state it more clearly, okay? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: My name is Neven Segaric. I come from Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Segaric, did you provide a witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in September of 2000?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And on December 3rd of last year - that's 2005 - did you have an occasion to review that witness statement in the presence of an officer of the Court, and did you sign a declaration attesting to its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Segaric's witness statement was admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber's decision of 16 January 2006, under 92 bis. It's been assigned exhibit number 251. With the assistance of the usher, I brought hard copies of this statement, the exhibit and the translation into English, for the Trial Chamber and Defence in case you would like to follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And Your Honours, according to the usual procedure for 92 bis witnesses, I'll first read a summary of the witness's statement. Afterwards, I'll have some follow-up questions before tendering the witness for cross-examination. And before I begin my summary I would also direct the Trial Chamber's attention to page 30 of the atlas which is Exhibit 23. The village of Skabrnja appears in grid A1, which is approximately 15 kilometres to the east of Zadar, just to help you locate the relevant area. I'll now begin my summary. The witness Neven Segaric is a Croat who at the time of these events was 11 years old and living in the village of Skabrnja, Croatia. About one month before Skabrnja was attacked in November 1991, the witness and most of the other villagers left and went to Preko Island for about one month. There the witness heard the cease-fire had been signed and after that he and others returned to Skabrnja. In the days before the attack on Skabrnja in November 1991, the witness could see the JNA around the village and there were more airplanes and helicopters flying in the area than usual. He also saw tanks pass by on the main road. For several days before the attack, the witness was spending the nights in the cellar of his uncle's house along with several relatives and neighbours, including two children a few years older than he was. At around 7.30 in the morning on the day of the attack, the witness saw a tank and soldiers in the area. He immediately told his father, who is a village guard. His father left for his guard post, telling the witness to stay in the cellar where he had been spending the nights. Some minutes later, a shell hit that house where the cellar was located but no one was injured. Shortly thereafter, someone started banging on the cellar door and asking who was inside, threatening to throw in grenade if they did not come out. One of the men in the cellar, Josip Miljanic, opened the door and about ten armed and uniformed JNA soldiers entered the cellar. Josip Miljanic was taken out for about ten minutes but then he was returned to the cellar. After that, Serb volunteers from neighbouring villages arrived at the cellar. These Serbs cursed the witness and the others saying, "Come out, you Ustasha. We are going to slaughter you all." Everyone was forced out of the cellar except for the witness's 62-year-old grandmother, Lucija Segaric. One of the Serbs fired his weapon into the cellar and some minutes later, when the witness was sent back into the cellar briefly, he saw that his grandmother was dead. Again outside the cellar, the witness saw Josip Miljanic and another neighbour named Stana Vickovic, 60 and 50 years old respectively, being forced to kneel down. A soldier wearing a camouflage uniform with SAO Krajina on the shoulder then shot them both in the head, killing them. The witness then saw several Serbs beating his 60- or 61-year-old grandfather Krsto Segaric. All of them were wearing green camouflage uniforms with SAO Krajina written in Cyrillic on the shoulder of the uniform. One of the men shot the witness's grandfather in the back of his head, killing him. At some point the witness also saw that one of the children, Ivo Bilaver, had been shot in the leg. The Serb soldier who had killed the witness's grandfather then asked the witness some questions about a number of people from the village. Then the soldier who had killed Josip Miljanic and Stana Vickovic grabbed the witness and his cousin Zeljko and pushed them against the wall of the house. The witness thought that he would be killed but a JNA officer intervened, saying, "There has been enough killing and we will not kill children." The JNA officer then took the witness and the two other children, Zeljko and Ivica, to the entrance of the village where they were put into a van and driven away. As they left the village, the witness saw a military column of tanks, APCs, cars and soldiers which was at least one kilometre long. The witness was then taken to Gornje Biljane where he and his cousin Zeljko were put into an elementary school while Ivo Bilaver was taken to hospital. After about one hour a 14-year-old boy named Denis Gurlica was also brought to the school and the witness saw other people who had been beaten and who were loaded into a truck and taken away. Around noon or 1 p.m., the witness, his cousin Zeljko, and Denis Gurlica were taken to another place, put into the back of a refrigerated truck, where their hands were tied and they were questioned. Finally, at about 3 p.m., the witness and the two other boys were taken to Benkovac where they joined others who had been captured in Skabrnja. Later that evening, the witness and the others were taken to a kindergarten in Benkovac, where they spent the night. There a Serbian television crew filmed the people who had been captured in Skabrnja. On the next morning, of 19 November, the witness and others captured in Skabrnja were exchanged into custody of the Croatian army and the witness was reunited with his family. The witness later learned that after the attack, his 94-year-old great-grandmother, Maja Grgica Segaric, was found shot to death in the witness's house in Skabrnja. That completes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, have you able to follow what I've been summarising from your statement?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you came to The Hague the first time a couple of weeks ago, did you have an opportunity to read your statement again, to review it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you point out to me one or two corrections that should be made to the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to hand the witness a hard copy of the Exhibit 251, which I've opened to the first page of his statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, if you please look at page 4 of that statement, you'll see a reference to a person called Stanko Miljanic. Do you find that? Is that the correct -- is that name correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: No. It's not correct. It should say Marko Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3 of your statement, it's written that Josip Miljanic had a weapon in the cellar. Do you find where it says that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: That's inaccurate. Josip Miljanic didn't have weapons. But my late grandfather and my father did, but that was on the second storey of the house. When the Chetniks went through the house, they were searching for pistols and rifles. There were two rifles upstairs and there were no rifles at all in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what kind of rifles were they, do you remember, the ones that were found upstairs?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Those were hunting rifles that my father and grandfather had licences for. They were stashed away there and would be taken out only in hunting season.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other corrections that needed to be made to your statement?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: There shouldn't be any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You can put that to the side for the moment now, although you may be asked about it later. Now I'm going to ask you a few additional questions about the events of that day in November 1991. First of all, are you able to tell us the date of the attack on Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the attack, was there any kind of warning or ultimatum given?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: No. There was no ultimatum and there were no indications that there was going to be an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In your statement you mentioned that your father and another man had been guarding the village during the night. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were. They were standing guard during that night on the eve of the fall of Skabrnja. In the morning, they were supposed to come back to their homes, but as the attack was launched, they returned to their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was there a village guard in Skabrnja at that time? Did other people guard the village besides your father and this other person that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were others. They were villagers, neighbours, relatives, people from the village. I don't know how many were standing guard that day but, yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about how this guard was organised?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I was a child back then, and I wasn't interested in that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand. Do you know if any of the other people who were with you in the cellar on the morning of the attack, were any of those other people members of this village guard?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: No, none of them. All of them were older people. I think Joso Miljanic was the eldest. He was 65. And I was the youngest. And for the most part these were women.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know the age -- do you know how old Ivica Bilaver was at the time of these events?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I think he was 14 or 15. That goes for Zeljko Segaric too. They were born in the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, with the assistance of the usher, I'm going to hand you some colour photocopies of some photographs. And there are three different bundles there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ERNs of these are 04687798 to 7815, the next one 04687816 to 7828, and finally, 04687829 to 7854. Your Honours, I'll also show these on e-court as we get to each booklet but I wanted to the witness to have hard copies because I think it will be easier to follow along. Your Honour, as to the time of the break, given the desire to finish this witness today, would it be possible to have 20-minute breaks today instead of 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe there is no need to change the schedule. We are going to finish today for sure. The Defence will finish its cross-examination on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To allow the Bench to ask these questions and the questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For sure, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the indication from the Defence. In that case, Your Honour, maybe it's an appropriate time for a break right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break now and come back at quarter to 11. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, just before the break, I had handed you some colour photocopies. I'd like you just to look through those three bundles quickly and tell me if you recognise those images. Yes, those are the ones.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: These are two photographs. To the left is our church. The photo was taken in the month of August, during a festivity we had. And the church you see on the right-hand side is the one that was blown up, blasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Segaric -- it's my fault. I'll ask you a few questions before we actually get to each booklet, but generally do you recognise those booklets? Have you seen those before?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, do you have copies for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't. They are going to be on the e-court. I hope that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll get them up there in just a moment. I just wanted to establish the authenticity before I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, did you in fact provide these three booklets of photos to me a couple weeks ago when you came to The Hague for the first time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And how did you yourself obtain these booklets of photographs? And just for clarity, you know, these are colour photocopies of booklets that you gave me, but how did you obtain the ones that you had, the originals?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: A neighbour of mine, Zoran Bulica had them. He is also a resident of Skabrnja. I don't know how he came by these pictures, but at any rate he gave them to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm going to now ask you to look through each one of them. And let's start with the one that has a typed page on the front page. And that has the ERN number 04687829 on the front page. If we could pull that up on e-court as well. It's the one that has -- no a different one.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: This is the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the front. Mot the blue one but the third one. Sorry, Mr. Segaric, it's in the other pile, on the right-hand side. That's the one I mean. If you could just check to make sure that at the top right, I think, it has a number 04687829 on the front page. Do you see a number like that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it showing on your screen? It's not showing on mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. That's correct, Your Honour. The first page is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page on the e-court, and Mr. Segaric, it's the second page titled, I think, "Description of photographs." Now, is the information on this page correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: No. It's inaccurate. To a large extent, in fact. I believe there is just two details that are correct and all the rest is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. How specifically is it incorrect? Can you tell me what's incorrect about it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: The numbers of the photographs don't tally. For instance, there is mention of a person that's not shown on the photograph here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Are some of the names on this page correct? Even if they don't match up with the correct photograph?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of them are, except for F4, Kljako Segaric and Krsto Segaric. The name is not Kljako, it's Kljajo. Therefore the name is wrong. Or, for instance, the body of Grgica Segaric. We called her Maja. She was my grandmother but there is no photograph of hers here. And Branko Rogic, there is no photograph of him. And Lucija Segaric as well, my grandmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I know that this is difficult and unpleasant but I'm going to ask you to look through these photographs, okay? We are going to go page by page and I just want you to tell us whatever you can about the photographs on each page. So let's turn the page now.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: This documentation on the -- concerning the on-site investigation, I have nothing to comment on in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just wait for one minute. Our computer system is lagging a little bit behind us, I think. We should be seeing page 04687831 now. Can you see that on the screen as well as in the hard copy? Is that the page you say you have no comment on?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, let's pass to the next page

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have no comment to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to the next page of this booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just mention that these first I believe four pages of this booklet have been translated into English, and that's also available on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could just scroll down to the bottom of that, and Mr. Segaric, look at the bottom of the two photos. Do you know what is represented there, what that is?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: This is the sign of their Ministry of the Interior. Most probably of the police administration of Benkovac, public security station Benkovac. This is their stamp, as far as I can read the Cyrillic. This is their documentation, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we move to the next page, please, and begin to see some of the photographs in this booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just say that these are graphic images, just so you know what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, what can you tell us about the three photographs on this page, if anything? You can look on the hard copy in front of you if it's easier.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: For example, the man lying on his back is my neighbour, Ante Razov, also known as Brico. He was the barber in our village, and he was killed. Now this house is the house of my uncle, Slavko Segaric. And these are the bodies of my grandfather and another person is Miljanic, and that's the cellar of the house I was captured in. The third image shows Soka Rogic, who was run over by a tank. And she was in this other shelter. These photographs must have been taken after we were captured, perhaps a day later, because I can see that the body of my late grandfather had been moved. He was lying on his side when I saw him last, and here we can see that he's on his back. Stana Vickovic and Joso Miljanic are the bodies of those killed here in front of this shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Segaric. On the computer screen, could we move back up to the centre photograph, please, which I think is the one. Is that the one you're referring to with your grandfather and the neighbours that you just mentioned, Mr. Segaric?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The photograph that has F2 written next to it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we move to the next page in the booklet, please. Are these the same photographs that were on the previous page, Mr. Segaric? I'm at the page now on our computer screen with --

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. With 04687834 on the top. Is that the right one that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to the next page on the e-court, please. Are those two more views of your uncle's house and your grandfather, Josip Miljanic and Stana Vickovic that you've discussed before?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the house belonging to Slavko Segaric, my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move to the next page, please. And again those are close-up photos of the people that you discussed on the prior pages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks for your patience, Mr. Segaric. The next page, please. This is more close-up photos of a person you mentioned. What was this person's name again?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: This person that was run over on the road is Soka Rogic. The person next to her is Kljajo Segaric. And these two persons are Rade Segaric and Joja Brkic. Josip Brkic, nicknamed Joja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, that's the page with ERN stamp 04687837. Can we pass --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you pass, I think the witness is identifying four people on that picture. I can only see three unless --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think the future pages may clarify, Your Honour. Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, who are the people shown in that first photograph with F4 next to it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: That is -- I mean the one lying down closer to us, that's Kljajo Segaric, and the one above him is Rade Segaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could look at the next photograph down on the page, please. Who is that, F5?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: That is Rade Segaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just scroll down to the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the same person as the other one on top?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It's a different photograph of the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the person in photograph marked F6, Mr. Segaric, who is that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: That's Joso -- I beg your pardon, Joso Brkic, nicknamed Joja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could pass to the next page, please. Those are more pictures of the same people you've just mentioned, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we pass to the next page, please. This next page will be 04687840, for the record. Perhaps with e-court for these next couple of pages, rather than zooming in on each photo, if we can just show the whole page I think it might go a little faster, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, are these more photos of two of the people you just named?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the picture up here, that is Ilija Razov. I confused him with Rade Segaric. The upper picture, the one that was in this group, that is Ilija -- Ilija Razov, that's what we called him. And Josip Brkic is the one down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So the picture F5A you're making a correction. You misnamed that person before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the correct name is Ilija Razov?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Let's pass to the next page, please. Can you tell who that is, Mr. Segaric?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: That's also Joso Brkic, nicknamed Joja, from the previous picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we pass to the next page now. For this, if we could zoom in a little bit so that we can see all three photographs, it would be helpful. And Mr. Segaric, if it helps you, you can look at the hard copies in front of you. Do you recognise any of the people in photographs F7, F8 and F9?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. F8 is Rade Segaric. Rade Segaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And can you tell if that's also the person in F7? Or if you can't tell, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I cannot -- I cannot tell myself. I know that F8 was Rade Segaric but F7 I cannot recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Any comment on F9?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: That is the shelter, the next basement, where they were taken prisoner, in the house of Peso Pavicic and his son, Mile Pavicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who was taken prisoner there, do you know?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: The mother and quite a few relatives and neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think we can pass to the next page, please. I think we can go ahead and pass to the next, please. Pass to the next page, please. Sorry, these are repeat photographs from before. This is a page marked 04687845. It says F9A next to the photograph. Mr. Segaric, do you know anything about this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I just know that this is the yard of Peso Pavicic, where his house was and where they were taken prisoner, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we move, there is something that looks like a person lying prostrate there. Is that a person or what is it? In blue and black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, are you able to answer His Honour's question? Is that a person there; and if so, do you know who that person is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The object in blue and black, next to something white there, that look like stones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell. I know that it is a corpse but I cannot recognise the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, that's fine. Can we pass to the next photograph, please. The next page. This is a page 04687846. Mr. Segaric, can you tell us anything about these photographs and who those people are, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: F10 and F11 is one and the same picture. That is Mile Pavicic, also taken prisoner and liquidated. F12, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next page, please. Are those the same pictures -- pictures of the same person we saw in the previous page?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same person, Mile Pavicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we pass to the next page, please. And to the next page as well. Mr. Segaric, do you know anything about these three photos or who these people are?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I do not know these persons. So I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we pass to the next page, please. Actually, Mr. Segaric, could you look at the remaining couple of pages there and see if there are any photographs that you do have comment on. Otherwise, we can finish with this booklet. Just go ahead and look at the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you repeat that. The interpreters couldn't hear it because I think the page hit the microphone. Just repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I have no comment with regard to the rest of the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for your patience in going through those.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this booklet receive an exhibit number and be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The booklet is received into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next two booklets, I think we can go through them much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, the booklet that's in front of you now that has a photo of a church on the front page and the word "Skabrnja." If you could just confirm for me that it has the number at the top 04687816. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And earlier when we first looked at the booklets, you started to describe what was shown on the front page. Could you please tell us now what's shown on that front page. If we could also see this on the e-court, that would be helpful, please.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: The left-hand picture, that's the church in Skabrnja. The picture was taken August 1991. That is when we have our fete. And on the right-hand side is the church as it was destroyed during the war, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever see, yourself, the church in this destroyed state?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I first returned to the village in October-November 1995. That's when I found the ruins of our church.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now what I'd ask the usher to do, if this is possible, it's just to go ahead and go through each page of this booklet, and we'll just go through and I'd ask the witness to look at them and then at the end I'll ask you about what's in there. Next page, please. If I could stop you there. This is page 04687818. Mr. Segaric, what's shown on that page?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: On the upper photograph, on the upper photograph, is the church of the Assumption of the Virgin, and on the lower picture is the church as it was destroyed, in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is this the same church that's shown on the cover of this booklet?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's the same picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can proceed now going through the booklet. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: The two upper pictures is our elementary school, Vladimir Nazor, in Skabrnja, that was blown up, torched but, thank God, it has been renewed now. And the lower picture is their emblem, Serb emblem, and it says, "God forgives, we do not. Welcome to a dead village." That is what they wrote during the occupation of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And we could go to the next page. Does the next page show the school as it's been rebuilt?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the rebuilt school in Skabrnja; the upper photograph and the lower photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could just again now look through the rest of the booklet and see if there is anything that you want to point out to us; otherwise, we can move on to the next booklet.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. St. Luke's church.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the number at the top of that page is?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If that page could be shown on e-court, please. I'm sorry, I interrupted you, Mr. Segaric. What were you telling us about the images on this page?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: On the upper photograph is our church; and the lower photograph, the second one, too; and the third one is St. Luke's church. That is where our cemetery is that was devastated. And the church was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear, there are two different churches in Skabrnja; the one that's shown on the front page and then this other one, St. Luke's church, which is shown in the bottom photograph of this page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other pages in the booklet that you want to comment on?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: On page 04687826.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And what would you like to say about that page?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: On the upper photograph is a mass grave near the elementary school. That is to say, in the centre of the village. That is where 30 to 40 villagers were buried. And on the lower picture you can see the destroyed cemetery by St. Luke's church.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. In the mass grave, where you said 30 to 40 villagers were buried, if you know, when were those 30 to 40 villagers -- when were they killed?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: They were killed between the 18th and 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any other pages in that booklet you would like to comment on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What's shown on that page?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: On all three you see the destroyed, demolished cemetery by St. Luke's church.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just -- is there anything else you want to discuss in that booklet?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I've said whatever I was supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that receive a number and be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document -- booklet be admitted into evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, there is just one more booklet I'd like to ask you to look at, and we are going to look at it very quickly. It's -- the front page is blue and it says "Skabrnja 1991 to 1996." The ERN of this document is 04687798 to 7815. And Mr. Segaric, if you could just look through the pictures in that booklet, all of them, and tell me what's depicted in those photographs.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Demolished houses in Skabrnja can be seen here. They were destroyed during the war, and when we got back, that's the way we found them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps on e-court, as the witness is looking at these, we could also flip through for the benefit of the Judges and the parties, please. So Mr. Segaric, when you returned to Skabrnja in 1995, did Skabrnja look the way it's represented in the photographs in this booklet?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I came back, it was destroyed. All the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you identify your uncle's house on any of these photographs in the booklet, where you were taken from the cellar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could see that page on the e-court, please. 7804. Where on this page does your uncle's house appear, Mr. Segaric?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: The lower picture on the left-hand side is the house of Nedeljko Segaric first, and then the one after it is Slavko Segaric's house, where I was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this booklet also receive a number and be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The booklet is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 272, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Segaric. And Your Honours, that took a little longer than I intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But I just have one more short topic, Mr. Segaric, and then the Defence will have some questions for you. After the attack on Skabrnja, do you know if the events, the attack, were ever reported in the media in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember anything specifically, where you know that it was reported?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: It was written about in the newspapers and it was on television that there was a massacre in Skabrnja, that 40 to 80 people were killed, and that 80 people were taken prisoner. That was on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember where you saw that in television, where you were, or what television station you saw it on?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you ask me about Croatian television or Serb television?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually either one. Croatian television or Serb television. Any place that you saw this reported.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: On Croatian television, it said that a Croatian village had been destroyed and that the villagers had been killed. And on Serb television it said that the Ustashas had massacred their own people. And in the evening, a TV crew came to a kindergarten - I think it was TV Knin - and then they reported -- we saw that on the following day -- that in Skabrnja, a crime had been committed by the Ustashas. That is to say that the villagers had killed themselves, that they had killed their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This may seem like an obvious question, but was that true, that the Ustashas had killed people in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: No. There were never any Ustashas in Skabrnja. Chetniks were in Skabrnja, who killed the villagers of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One last question: Did you ever hear about any investigation or prosecution by the Serb authorities for the crimes that happened in Skabrnja which you told us about here today?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard anything of the sort. I was in Benkovac and I was interrogated at the police administration by the police officers there. They questioned me but there was no sort of investigation about the events in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What day was that that you were interrogated in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: That was on the 18th of November, in the evening, when I arrived in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you -- did you tell them about the things that you've told us here today? About what had happened to your family and your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: No. They never asked me about that. They asked me about weapons and such like, how many Ustashas there were in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But they didn't ask you any questions about what had happened to your family and your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: No, nobody asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Segaric. Your Honours, no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the cross-examination of the witness will be done by co-counsel, Nikola Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Segaric.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You have heard I'm one of the counsel for Mr. Martic and I will now start my cross-examination. Based on your personal details, I learned that you were born on the 14th of June 1980.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, prior to the events you testified about, you were 11 years old in -- at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel for the Prosecution please switch off the mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You gave your statement to the Prosecution in 2000; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore nine years after the events that transpired?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In this statement to the OTP, you yet give information in great detail about the numbers of soldiers there, about the time line of the events. You also provide them with the information about the numbers of the tanks and other vehicles. In connection with this, I have a question. How come you were able to remember all these details with such precision after nine years?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: You see, I never gave an exact number. I always gave rough figures. And as I was appearing before a court every year and a half, I was compelled to remember these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, you state that the basement where you were in, that first a group of ten or so members of the JNA, wearing olive-drab uniforms, entered the basement. What did they tell you, to you who were in the basement?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: First of all, when they approached the house, we could hear noise, the din of them trying to enter the room. Then they asked for the door to be opened. Joso Miljanic then opened the door, but the first -- at first, when the soldiers came, individual soldiers told us that they would not harm us, that we would not get killed, and things along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, they didn't threaten you.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Others threatened us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the soldiers only.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I said that some of them comforted us, others threatened us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: They left after that, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You next state that, after them, and now I'm quoting your words: "Serbian volunteers, villagers of the neighbouring villages appeared, who used disparaging remarks and cursed you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how long it was after the JNA soldiers left that these people came?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: It's hard to say. May have been half an hour or ten minutes. We weren't thinking about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You stated that they were searching for weapons and that they were asking after persons who they suspected had weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may also add, they also asked, they asked not only about weapons but about houses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the annex to your statement, dated 13th of March 2006, you stated that they found hunting weapons belonging to your father and grandfather in the attic of your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not in the attic. That's a room. Although that may seem to be an attic, that's just upstairs from where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You went on to say that Stana Vickovic and Josip Miljanic were killed by a man wearing a camouflage uniform who had a patch of the SAO Krajina on his arm and that you saw that.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise the man?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I recognised quite a few people because they -- it was a neighbouring village, but I can't recall the name. I only remember their faces and I remember that I found their faces familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that these soldiers wearing green camouflage uniforms with the Cyrillic SAO Krajina on their arm also wore red five-pointed stars; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but the signs were mixed. There were those wearing Serb signs, there were those wearing red stars. They were all mixed together, those wearing red stars and those wearing Serb signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, the red five-pointed star, did it symbolise the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, on the photographs shown to you by the Prosecutor, rather, the F1, F1A, F1B, and F2, one can see that they are a result of an on-site investigation of, as it is said, unidentified dead bodies in Skabrnja that was conducted on the 21st of November 1991 by the police in Benkovac. Do you know whether it was the SAO Krajina Police, in fact?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the police officers from Benkovac who conducted the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I didn't see anyone conducting any on-site investigation that day, and I can't tell you whether one was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You saw the photographs. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You see that they bear the sign of the Benkovac police station and the sign of the SAO Krajina. If you cannot give any definite answer, I will not insist.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question. You want me to say that this stamp is the stamp of SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: The people from Benkovac who conducted the on-site investigation, were they members of the police of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I have another question. Do you know that the TV Knin was established in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN SEGARIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I remember very well that they had their report, that it was broadcast on TV Knin by the Serbian TV at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Segaric, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. No questions from the Bench. I beg your pardon. Any re-examination, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, thank you very much, Mr. Black. Witness, thank you so much for coming. We appreciate your coming and giving your evidence. We are finished with you. You are excused and you may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm informed that the next witness won't be ready until 12.30. I didn't anticipate that this would go near so quickly. I don't know -- he would be at the hotel currently. I don't know if there is any chance of bringing him here -- I don't think before 12.00 when we were scheduled for the next break. So I apologise, Your Honour, I think we are going to lose the next 18 minutes of court time. But he'll be ready to start the third session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, can we take an adjournment and come back at half past 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned to come back at half past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Can you hear me clearly in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I can hear you clearly and I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, please state your name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Marko Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Are you of Croatian nationality?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Croat, yes, by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Were you born in 1951?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Are you presently retired?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Before retiring, what kind of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Ministry of the Interior, and before that, a member of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What was your position in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: In the JNA, I was a junior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Until when were you a junior officer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Up until the 15th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Under what circumstances did you leave the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: When the unrest started and after the murder of the police officers at Borovo Selo and at Plitvice, I decided to leave the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you tell us why, in a bit more detail.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Because I could see that this was no longer the Yugoslav People's Army but that it has rather -- that it had rather sided with just one party, and that's to say with the Serb side. I, as a member of the Croatian people, could not take part in something that was leveled against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, where were you living in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I was living in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you have the occasion to visit the village of Skabrnja before 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: My parents, brothers and sisters, all lived in Skabrnja. I left Skabrnja in 1966. Zadar is some 14 to 15 kilometres away from Skabrnja, and I'd use any spare time I had and I would go to Skabrnja at the weekends and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. And by the way, do you know Mr. Ante Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Ever since 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How do you know him, in brief terms?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I know him superficially. I was a member of the MUP and he was a member and commander of the Croatian army, but we would come across each other in Zadar. Zadar is not that large a town, some 100.000 people, and our paths would cross. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And does this have any effect on your testimony here today, Mr. Miljanic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, no effect at all. What I'm about to testify now happened in 1991, whereas, as I said, I met Mr. Gotovina for the first time in 1993. Therefore, one has nothing to do with the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Witness, I'd now like to ask you some questions about the village of Skabrnja. What was the approximate population of Skabrnja in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: In 1991, there were about 2.000 inhabitants in the village of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the inhabitants of Skabrnja at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Skabrnja was an exclusively Croat village. Catholic population, and by ethnicity they were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Were there any military installations in the village of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: There had never been any military installations of any sort in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What about the surrounding villages in the area? How would you characterise them in terms of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The other villages were as follows: The southern villages, or to the south of Skabrnja, had only Croat population. Some villages surrounding Skabrnja had some Serb population, that's Zemunik, then Milane -- Biljane and Nadin. Biljane was an exclusively Serb village whereas Nadin had some Serb population but 90 per cent of them were Croats. As for Donji Zemunik, there was mixed population there as well. That's about 10 kilometres away from Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now like to ask you about certain events in the fall of 1991. On the 5th of September 1991, what were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of September 1991, I was called by the chief of the then-Zadar police administration, Mr. Ivica Brzoja, and gave me the following order -- actually, I received a written and verbal order to secure, as a police officer, that peace be maintained throughout the area and that there is operating communication in the area, although there was communication at the time, there was even Lieutenant Mladic in the area, and that I should make sure that the provisions of the cease-fire agreement that had been reached in The Hague be strictly adhered to. Those were the orders I was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come to that agreement later. Did you undertake at this time to organise anything in the village? Of Skabrnja, that is.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I did, but before that, I have to say that the entire population of Skabrnja, on the 2nd of October 1991, after heavy bombing, had been all moved out of the village. That's to say all the population was moved out; the elderly people, women and children. The only persons left in the village were men, men of younger age. Once the cease-fire was agreed upon, the entire population of Skabrnja was taken back to their village from Zadar. They were transported in five buses back to their home village. The men resumed their work posts that they had in Zadar, and there were no provocations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. But I want to go back a bit. When you were called by the chief of the then police administration and he gave you an order and you were assigned a task. Was there anything specifically that you organised in the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: In the village itself, since we had already been exposed to bombing and missiles by the army and the paramilitaries, whoever was there, I make sure that we identified basements in the village where the civilians could find shelter, if need be, and we identified eight such basements in the village of Skabrnja which was supposed to be used as shelters in the event of bombing or missiles being launched. And we placed check-points near Biljane and Zemunik along the road there, and that's what I organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt a little bit? I'm not quite sure, are we talking about Skabrnja or are we talking about Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: We are talking about Skabrnja, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, I would just like to clarify something with you. You've just told us about identifying basements to be used as shelters and check-points being placed. Which village are you referring to in regard to these activities?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Skabrnja. I'm referring to Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have certain equipment in Skabrnja; and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: You're probably referring to weapons. Yes. We did. I have to tell this Honourable Trial Chamber that we had six light machine-guns, two hand-held launchers, some 50 rifles. Some of these were trophy weapons, dating back from World War II, some of them were M-48 rifles. There were some that were semi-automatic, some were automatic. We had some pistols, and we had some ammunition too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who are the "we"? We had -- we had six light --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We, the inhabitants of the village of Skabrnja who were members of the reserve police force. So we are talking about members of the reserve police force and volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And approximately how many such members and volunteers did you have in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: 242 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier, Witness, you spoke about villagers being evacuated. Can we go back to this? Can you tell us when that was again?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: This happened on the 2nd of October 1991. Let me explain the situation. On that day, three villagers of Skabrnja got killed. At that point I decided, in agreement with the Crisis Staff of Zadar municipality, to pull out all the civilians and evacuate them to the islands overlooking Zadar, and it was then that all of them were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And tell us again who remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The ones that I mentioned, 240 people stayed behind, including a priest and a teacher, and, of course, myself. We stayed back in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And why did you remain? Of all the people who remained, that is, why did you all remain?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: We didn't want to abandon the place because, before that, we were exposed to bombing every day and we had, of course, livestock, we had our land. We were farmers, and we dared not leave our village because we did not wish to lose the properties that we had and, of course, we wanted to guard our own village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Of the men who remained, how old were they? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: On average, the people were aged 30 to 35. There were some who were older. I myself was 42 at the time, but I was the oldest. All the other ones were younger than me. I was among the older ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miljanic, were you at around this time aware of soldiers leaving the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, because more than 80 JNA soldiers came to me personally and told me that they had fled the JNA. They came to me in my village and I sent them, all of them, to Zadar.
