Among them were soldiers of all ethnicities, including Croats, Hungarians, Albanians, Slovenians and Serbs; of all ethnicities. They came to me. They were on the run from Benkovac, and they told me that there was real chaos up there. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Have you heard the names Dean Brener and Captain Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were also with me. But Mr. Sveljo, who was a police officer at the time, was also with them, and this is something that was not stated. They seemed suspicious and they were brought over to me from the check-point. I interrogated them. I knew Petar Sveljo from before the war. He told me that they had basically strayed. I escorted them over to Zadar, and I know what happened with them next, roughly, but, of course, I'm here to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, do you know who Mr. Brener was?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I do because I asked him. He introduced himself at first with a false name. I remember still that he introduced himself as Esad Catic and told me that he was a resident of Bihac and that he was the chef of the restaurant in Benkovac. I knew who was working in the kitchen of that restaurant in Benkovac and I simply caught him in this lie, and he then admitted that he wasn't Esad Catic but Captain Dean Brener, commander of the tank company stationed in Biljane and that -- Veljane, and that the person with him was from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the person's name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I found out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the person who was from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Captain Jovanovic. I don't recall his first name. I only know that he was the commander of the infantry company also stationed in Veljane. I don't know if that's the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, did you have a conversation with Mr. Brener?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We talked for more than an hour and he told me -- and I have to use this expression before this Honourable Trial Chamber -- that we were going to lose it, that we're done for, and that Ratko Mladic was going to defeat us. And he also told us that the Chetniks had arrived from Serbia and that we had better run from Skabrnja to Zadar for our lives. I told him to take care of his own business and not to meddle into this, but in retrospect, I think I should have listened to what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When he mentioned Ratko Mladic to you, did you know who that person was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I did. I repeat, I was a member of the army. I worked in Zadar but my base or HQ was in Knin. I often went to Knin and I got to know Ratko Mladic, although this was only in passing. I was told that this colonel - he was a colonel at the time - had arrived from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you about certain other events. On the 5th of November 1991, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: On the 5th, The Hague truce was signed. That's to say on the 5th of November, 1991. When I was invited to come to Mr. Ivan Brzoja, chief of the police administration, who gave me a written and a verbal order, to the effect that The Hague truce was signed and that we ought not to provoke. I replied to this by telling him, "Chief, we have nothing to provoke with. Can we really provoke the air force with the rifles we have?" He told me, "I'm going to hold you responsible for this. You're a member of the police administration." I went about my business and things went back to normal, people resumed their jobs in the factory. However, the following day, on the 6th -- or rather, on the following day, on the 6th, the people were taken back to Skabrnja on five buses, and life resumed as per normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: The instruction that you were given not to provoke, to what extent was it followed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: To the full extent. I repeat before this Honourable Trial Chamber, to the full extent. Not a single bullet had ever been fired. We didn't even have much ammunition. We each had maybe 15 bullets, and we could not afford to provoke. At that time, Ratko Mladic was passing in a vehicle to Zadar for negotiations and he was accompanied by Brener at the time and nobody hindered his passage in any way. There was a truce on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, I'd now like to turn to the events of the 18th of November, 1991. Can you tell us what happened on the 18th of November, 1991, starting from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I find it quite hard to talk about these events. Very hard. I lost half my family on that day. I lost some of my best friends. I saw my father's throat slit on that day. But I will recount everything as it happened, only the truth, as I said at the outset. On that morning, I was sleeping in a house in the centre of the village by the radio set we had. It was this ordinary police radio set. The lad who was seated by the radio set, I asked him whether there was anything new to report about? He told me, No, Marko, there is nothing new. At about 7.30, tanks could be heard from the direction of Benkovac. At that point, since I had people at Razovljeva Glavica, which is an elevation above Skabrnja, standing guard, one of the men there informed me over a field telephone line that the tanks were arriving also from the direction of Gornje Zemunik, the airport there. I had three couriers of mine, and I sent them to inform the civilians to flee to their shelters, and to inform the police officers who were there to take their positions above the village. At that point - that was about 7.30, I don't recall the exact time - fierce artillery fire was opened upon the village from tanks and artillery pieces. The entire village was ablaze. Some 15 minutes later, from Veljane and Biljane, one could hear gun shots. One could hear them all around Skabrnja. I used the radio set to report on the situation to Zadar. I told them that we were under attack and we didn't know what was going on. I received a piece of information from this information centre in Zadar that we had, that people should run into shelters and that they weren't aware of what was going on. At that time, civilians were starting to get killed in the shelling. The physician we had in the village had to intervene already with two or three people. First of all, there was this lady, some 50 metres away from me, whose legs had been shattered by a shell. She was dying in great pain. Another lady next to her, too. And there was general chaos, nobody knew what was going on. I found out from the couriers who came to report to me that there was general chaos, that the tanks from Zemunik Gornje and Biljane were heading our way, and that's -- that was as far as I myself knew. We could hear the wailing of animals, people, in the general smoke and fire. All of a sudden, we could hear aircraft. At one point, about a kilometre away from where I was, in the direction of Donji Zemunik, I could hear helicopters. Infantry forces dismounted these helicopters. They were wearing dark uniforms. I didn't know who they were. I didn't know what was going on. At the time - this was around 11.00 - I heard -- I overheard on the radio set, as I stated to the investigators, a conversation between Colonel Cecovic, I knew from Benkovac, and Ratko Mladic. This was an open-type conversation. They were saying that their reserve ammunition supplies were destroyed. I don't know what was going on. I only heard this terrible explosion up on the road. There was this truck that was blown up, either by a shell or I don't know. At that point the attack subsided and Cecovic placed a call to Ratko Mladic and told him in these very words, "Comrade --" I'm not sure how he addressed him, I think "Comrade." "My reserve ammunition supplies have been destroyed. He told him in turn, "Go ahead. If you fail, I will execute you, Cecovic." And these are the very words I heard. In this general chaos, a young man came up to me, who later on got killed, that in my hamlet people were being killed, one by one. I asked him, are they in the basements? He answered, "Yes, they are in the basements but they are being taken out one by one and killed." I told him to tell them to run for the centre of the village if they can, and to abandon their shelters. Another man came to me subsequently and I asked about the young man who was previously reporting to me, and this man told me, well, he got killed. This person I was talking to at the time also got killed. His name was Ante Razov. In the presence of my mother, his ears were cut off and he was killed on the road. The army had already went ahead. It was those vultures that followed them, they did these things. At that point I lost track of time and everything. At that point, planes started firing cluster bombs. I have to tell you that even before, in the month of October, Skabrnja was bombed by these prohibited cluster bombs by the JNA. These were English cluster bombs that were fired upon the village of Skabrnja, indiscriminately.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you for a second. Just to be clear, just now you've explained to us what happened on the 18th and starting from early in the morning. You mentioned fierce artillery fire. Who was doing the firing? Do you know who was doing the firing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, as a soldier, I know who did this. The JNA went ahead. The JNA went ahead. And, gentlemen, whoever got into their hands that day is alive to this day, but they were conquering territory. They were going in tanks. So the JNA had tanks and cannons and aircraft and rocket launchers and everything at that time. But everyone knows who this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't. Can you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've said, the JNA was taking the terrain, the ground, and behind them went certain paramilitary or whatever forces that killed everyone. I am not a witness to that because I was out in that part of the village that had not been taken yet. But according to the stories that other people told my mother, who watched all of this, all these people who were there. I repeat, I did not witness that. I did not see it myself. So I cannot say something that I don't know. But I know what the JNA had.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more precise about the equipment and the manpower that the JNA was deploying that day.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The JNA on that day used all kinds of equipment. That is to say from the tactical equipment to strategic equipment. In the JNA, at that time, there was such a system of control and command at the time that it was known who would approve the use of what kind of weaponry. So the air force could only be used by the corps commander or someone of equal rank. For example, a tank brigade could be used only by the commander of the tank brigade. So we are not talking about marginal people. We are talking about people who were in highest positions of responsibility and who were in command at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what did this indicate to you? Did it indicate anything?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: This indicated everything to me. I'm telling you that. I was a member of that army for 22 years, 22 years. It was all clear to me. Quite simply, Skabrnja was not attacked from -- for any military reasons. No military reasons. Skabrnja was attacked for political interests and in order to intimidate, because on the same day, when Skabrnja was destroyed, that's when Vukovar was destroyed, and it was necessary to prove to all what would happen after the massacre in Skabrnja. Zadar had an unprecedented exodus. Up to 30.000 inhabitants of Zadar fled in the direction of Rijeka, Slovenia, and Italy, so Skabrnja was used as a political objective, not a military target in any way. That is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And tell us again, what kind of manpower did you have that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: On that day, I've already said, I had six submachine-guns. The calibre was, if you follow my drift, 7, 9 millimetres. I had two hand-held rocket launchers with four shells each. It is like a bazooka, if you understand that. The rest was mixed weaponry. So, some M-48 rifles, some trophy carbines, Italian ones from the Second World War. We also had some Kalashnikovs. I think -- well, they were few. And then we had about ten automatic rifles and ten to 15 pistols and four or five rifles that we had with small calibres that were at the school for training purposes, and that is what we had in Skabrnja. We did not have any heavy weaponry in Skabrnja, no heavy weaponry; no tanks, no cannons, nothing. And quite simply, even if we wanted -- well, I mean, resistance was put up. I have to say that. Well, people would not allow these things to happen. They would see people getting killed and attack, and any man was ready to defend his house, and that's what they did. But I have to say that it was an unequal fight. One to 1.000, gentlemen. One to 1.000. Not in terms of manpower, personnel, but in terms of material. Somebody has cannons, rocket launchers, aircraft, tanks, and somebody has rifles on the other hand. So that's what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned a conversation which you overheard between a colonel -- Colonel Mladic and Colonel Cecovic. Now, how did you know that the persons speaking were Colonel Mladic and Mr. Cecovic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I knew. First of all, I knew Colonel Cecovic well because he was brigade commander in Benkovac. And in the former army, I was commander of the construction engineering company and I had Benkovac within my maintenance. So I knew him personally. As for Ratko Mladic, I knew him because he spoke on television. Well, I knew him. Because they talked openly. It wasn't a scrambled conversation or coded. So they used this vocabulary very openly. In this basement where I sought shelter there were over 70 civilians. 60 to 70, I don't know any more; maybe 50, maybe 80, I don't know. They hid there and they were right next to me, and they all listened to what was being said over the radio. Gentlemen, I tried to get these civilians out of the basement so that they could flee towards Prkos. That was part of Skabrnja that had not been taken yet. But they didn't want to. They were crying and they were saying, "Why are you trying to get us out?" So I have witnesses, over 70 witnesses. Quite simply, they could not leave these basements because of the shelling, and many of them ended their lives, as everyone knows: Killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, you also mentioned seeing helicopters that day. Do you recall how many individuals emerged from each helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I cannot know, but I just know that three or four helicopters would come on three or four occasions. I don't know. People just got out. People that were closer to them, well, it's about a kilometre, even less than a kilometre, from me, and those who were closer were only 150 to 200 metres away. At the western part of Skabrnja there is a meadow called Jabuka. That is where the helicopters landed and soldiers disembarked from them and then moved around. I cannot give you an exact number but I can give you an estimate; about 30 people can fit into a helicopter, so then look into that. 30 people per helicopter, because I know that from the former Yugoslavia in the army. I remember I actually flew in a helicopter myself. We had exercises, training, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you see any tanks that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. Of course, I did. From Benkovac and from Gornje Zemunik, and then those that were -- there were those from Donji Zemunik, from the airport. I didn't see them but I heard over the radio people telling me that they were coming too and that they were encircling the village. They wanted to trap the village completely and not to let anyone leave this place alive. That was the objective. We learned about this in the army. It's called pliers. That's how you have a siege, and it's closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you at any point see anything happening near the tanks or around them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I just have to say one thing: I was not even 50 metres away from the tanks. That was in the afternoon, around 1400 hours. I came and Mr. Luka Skara did - he's still alive to this day - and two young men with a hand-held rocket launcher and one shell, to try to destroy the tank that entered the centre of the village. But regrettably, there were civilians all around the tank, on the sides and in front, with their hands on their necks and had we shot at this tank we would have killed those civilians around the tank. That's why I didn't have the courage to reach that kind of decision. So I did not shoot. But there were civilians all around the tanks and between them. The tanks were moving ahead; in front of them, women, children, old men, and between them. And we were standing by the church, the then church, because they destroyed it, they razed it to the ground afterwards. We stood by the church and we tried to hit this tank, but as I said, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Why do you think that there were civilians around the tank?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, because I saw it. I saw it with my very own eyes. Everybody saw it. All of those who were taken prisoner in Skabrnja who are alive to this day. They can all confirm this to you. They were all there with their hands on their necks, up here, and as I said the army -- well, in my opinion, in my understanding, I don't know whether this is correct, but the army saved those civilians, you see. Those who were captured by the army were saved.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know what else I could tell you. Quite simply, this was hell. Unheard of. I cannot think of this, remember this. These were such moments when animals in barns are burning; sheep, cows, horses, people are moaning. You see dismembered human bodies around you. The doctor, all bloodstained, ran up to me and said, What are we going to do? And this same doctor had terrible moments. Then the priest hid 50 people in a basement and they destroyed that house and they never found those people. This same priest, Don Tomislav Sikiric, got them out three days later. These were horrible moments. You could not see a thing. You could not hear anything from the shooting, from the mayhem all around. I could never have imagined something like that, that something like that could happen. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you know how many civilians were killed on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, because I don't know who was killed then and who was killed later, later. Because a group of civilians stayed behind near the school, 27 to 30 of them, and then in February 1992, they were all killed and put into a mass grave near the Skabrnja school. They were all killed. All of them who were taken prisoner. But I don't know exactly how many civilians were killed on that day. I just know what came to the Zadar pathology department. My father, my brother, seven relatives of mine, I met them on that day in black bags, and Your Honours, I just have one thing to say: An officer from here, from the Netherlands, was there in front of the Zadar pathology department. He started vomiting. He said that he had been through many wars in Indochina, whatever, but he had never experienced anything like this. So the man was vomiting five metres away from me because he saw terrible things that came in these black bags to the pathology department of the Zadar hospital, that came from Skabrnja. That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Of the persons who were engaging in the defence of the village that day, how many of them were killed, do you know, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: 15 or 16. I don't know. About 14 were taken prisoner, 15 got killed. I think 15 got killed. I didn't know. I didn't know about my brother. I did not know about my brother. I learned only four days later that he got killed. And to this day, I don't know exactly how many people got killed, or rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreter couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreter couldn't hear you just now, the last part of what you said. Would you mind repeating that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that I did not know the exact number on that day and the following three and four days. I did not know exactly how many people got killed in Skabrnja, because quite simply, it was impossible to know. Everybody was seeking their nearest and dearest. Some people were looking for their mother, their father, their brother, their sister. Everybody was looking in Zadar because people were scattered about, people had fled from Zadar. So this was chaos. This chaos that was sown on that day, this terror of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, did you at some point that day, on the 18th, did you hear someone named Petar Radmanovic speaking?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Petar Radmanovic worked with me in the former army. He was a warrant officer at the artillery school centre in Zadar. We were good friends. I heard him, but he was not issuing orders. He was just provoking me over the radio in a very ugly way. Using words that are quite inappropriate and that I would rather not repeat before this Honourable Trial Chamber. Cuss words, things like that, but I heard him. Terrible. All sorts of things. It amused him, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could you tell us how he was provoking you over the radio?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you that before this Honourable Trial Chamber, I simply cannot utter such words. The venue does not allow me to do so. But swearing at my mother, what would happen to me, that I would be hanged, and that they would take out my liver and grill it. Things like that. Everybody, all the civilians who were in the basement that time, heard that. These are horrible things, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness's microphone is off again, notes the interpreter. No microphone. The witness's microphone is still off, notes the interpreter. It just goes off.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I think the witness's mike is off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it all right now? May I? Your Honour, these are horrible things, truly horrible things, that a man that you worked with for years, that he sends you messages when in your native village everybody is being killed, that he's provoking you, that he swears at you, that he swears at my mother, that he calls me a derogatory term; an Ustasha. I was never an Ustasha. And then he says what he's going to do to me when he catches me alive and so on. But what can I tell you? Other people knew other people who were speaking. I didn't know anybody else. But they said that they recognised a former policeman. Well, later, a policeman of the SAO Krajina, Mr. Opacic. I don't know that. I didn't know him. I just knew him by sight, but I didn't know Mr. Opacic. Others said that it was his voice. This Mr. Opacic nicknamed Klempa. I don't know whether that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what happened after the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I had this radio link, this police radio link. Half of the village was taken by 1400 hours, and people were killed there, and I was in the other half of the village, and those people who fled to that side, towards the railway station. All of a sudden, two aircraft appear and they fire rockets and this radio station had an antenna on the oak tree. I didn't have any other equipment but this radio station on the oak tree, and the aircraft simply fired a rocket, cut this oak tree. I lost all channels of communications and I had no communications ever again with Zadar. So since they were listening to everything that was going on, Zadar itself was shelled and bombed then. According to the information that I received subsequently, they thought that I got killed at that moment, and they said, "That's it. Marko is not reporting any more. He's dead." But thank God, I stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, I just have a few more questions for you. Did you ever hear of any Serbian authorities in the SAO Krajina conducting an investigation into the killings that happened on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I didn't at the time, but later on, during Operation Storm, papers were found where the former police members in Zadar had conducted on-site investigations and five bodies were found in Petrovac. I had occasion to see that, as a police officer, and I was able to see photographs that I had never seen before; the body of my father, that of Mr. Segaric's, and of other bodies lying by a fence. Mr. Miljus had conducted the on-site investigation. This was Mr. -- this was signed by Mr. Miljus on behalf of the police administration in Benkovac. Now, whether an investigation was carried out or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And finally, Witness, do you recall giving a statement to a Croatian investigative judge, a Mr. Mikolcevic, in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I do. I remember that very well. But the statement was given under very difficult circumstances. On that same day, Zadar was under heavy shelling. On that day, right next to the police station where the prison is located, several shells landed in the immediate vicinity. Mr. Mikolcevic and the lady who was typing my statement out and I myself who was there had to stop the procedure. I could -- we could not continue. I signed the statement hastily and we agreed that we would meet again to complete the statement but we never did. I remember that day very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And do you recall roughly over how long a period of time this statement was given?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. Perhaps for an hour. I don't remember. Perhaps less, perhaps more. Well, it must have been more than an hour that we were in his office. This was on the second floor of the Court there, I remember. And then we had -- or rather, of the prison, where we had to run into the shelter that was in the basement, where coal supplies were usually stocked. But that's in the basement of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Valabhji. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the cross-examination of this witness will be done by Mr. Nikola Perovic, co-counsel in our team. Given the time, I'm not certain whether we should start today. We will definitely have to continue our cross-examination tomorrow, but it is in the Court's hands whether we should indeed perhaps start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We still have ten minutes, Mr. Milovancevic. I would suggest that we start now. I think let's make good use of these ten minutes that are remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, I suppose you know what this is about. I am one of the Defence counsel for the accused Martic and I will now start your cross-examination as provided for in our rules. I kindly ask you to make a short break before answering my questions in order to facilitate the work of the interpreters. You said that before you became employed with the Ministry of the Interior, or rather, the Zadar police force, you had spent 22 years of service within the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more -- in more detail what it was you did in the JNA, what your specialty was.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Right after I completed the military school, I went to the navy centre at Losinj, and I was the commander of the special purpose platoon, which meant that I had to deal with explosives, mines and so on and so forth, and I completed training for mining and dealing with minefields and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you were appointed commander of the defence of Skabrnja on the 26th of September, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 26th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who appointed you to that duty?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The chief of the police administration, Mr. Ivica Brzoja. He didn't appoint me, really, I was simply sent up there. I didn't receive an appointment or any written order, I was simply told to go up there and to organise these things so that people wouldn't be creating any problems, but I didn't receive any written order. I was sent over there for three days only, but I had to stay for longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, if I remember, you left the JNA in the month of May of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why does one start organising the defence of the village of Skabrnja in late September 1991? What were the reasons that led to this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Sir, this was because on the 15th of August, 1990, as early as then, there was arson committed in Skabrnja by the villagers of Biljane, and they started opening fire. That was the main reason why the people in Skabrnja started thinking about how to organise their defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that this was in August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I have a question in connection with this. So a year later you started organising defence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was throughout that year that we were experiencing atrocities. Five men had been killed in Skabrnja in the meantime. Two in Nadin and three in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, can I remind you, please, when counsel has asked a question, give a break before you answer, because you don't give the interpreters an opportunity to interpret. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, you go on to state that Skabrnja, Zemunik Gornje, and Nadin were attacked on the 2nd of October 1991 with artillery and infantry of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "enemy," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The JNA and the paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore the JNA that you served in for 22 years and that you left three months earlier, you consider it to be the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. It proved to be that because it sided with the Serb people against all the others, and automatically to me it was the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Miljanic -- or rather, do you remember who the Commander-in-Chief of the army was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any more. Probably I haven't been thinking about it. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What happened on the 10th of October, 1991, do you remember? To what post were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Which date again?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The 10th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I was appointed commander for the defence of all the seven villages at Ravni Kotari, and I will enumerate them now: Skabrnja, Nadin, Gornje Zemunik, Donji Zemunik, Prkos, Gorica, Karlovac and Glavica. Galovac, that's to say instead of Karlovac. That's a third of the municipality of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How many men did you have under your command in the area?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: 700 something men. 730, 740, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: There were no members of the National Guards Corps there, were there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No. There were only the locals there. I have to tell you that before that, in the village of Nadin, there was one platoon of the ZNG, which pulled out of Nadin on the 2nd of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In response to the question by the prosecutor, you explained, Mr. Miljanic, how many weapons you had.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned six submachine-guns, two hand-held rocket launchers, and you talked about other weapons. Now, in connection with this, I have the following question: Who armed the men who were under your command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Who armed them? Part of the weaponry, as I said, were trophy weapons and sports weapons. Some of the weapons were purchased by the people themselves in Slovenia. From different sources. The soldiers who fled the JNA, all 80 of them, gave their weapons to us up at Skabrnja. All the soldiers fleeing the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When I'm talking about weapons, I'm primarily referring to hand-held rocket launchers and mortars, as heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: When you head off from Gorski Kotar or Delnice -- or rather, the weapons were obtained from that particular area, by someone, I don't know who. I simply found the weapons there already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that these were pieces of weaponry from the barracks in Gorski Kotar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's my assumption and it doesn't have to be necessarily correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can I therefore conclude that the weapons were seized from these barracks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were surrendered, whether they were captured. I know that in some of the barracks, the army surrendered their weapons without any resistance. I can't tell you anything about that. I didn't take part in any negotiations or conversations. I was an ordinary police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we should finish for the day, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do agree, Mr. Perovic. The Court will adjourn now and will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
